description: Route and worker-batch performance budgets, keyed on METHOD /path (exact OpenAPI path template). Each entry declares the maximum database-call count, downstream-call count, response bytes, application latency and memory for one operation. Measured fields are populated by src/scripts/measure-route-budgets.mjs from a real measurement and are null until then. check-route-budgets.mjs validates structure, enforces every populated measurement against its ceiling, and reports coverage as a fraction of the whole route surface — never as a bare pass.

surface.criticalSelection: A route is critical when it is (a) issued on every authenticated page load, (b) the primary list or detail read of an in-scope module, (c) the primary transactional write of an in-scope module, or (d) a scheduled worker batch that iterates tenant data. Everything outside that set is declared-out-of-scope, not measured-and-passing.
surface.honesty: totalOperations is recomputed from openapi.json on every gate run. The value stored here is the count at the release commit; the gate prints the live number so the denominator can never go stale without being visible.

workerBatchScope.derivedFrom: every @Get/@Post operation on a @Controller("cron") class under src/, re-read by check-route-budgets.mjs on every run — not a list stored here
workerBatchScope.why: surface.criticalSelection names four clauses. (a), (b) and (c) are product judgements and stay asserted (R-13). (d) — "a scheduled worker batch that iterates tenant data" — is not a judgement: a scheduled batch in this codebase IS an operation on a cron controller, so the set is readable out of source. Deriving it turns "82 budgets, and we believe that is the critical set" into a countable fraction, which is the question this ticket's first box actually asks.
workerBatchScope.unit: one budget per PATH, not per HTTP method: GET /cron/x and POST /cron/x are the same private handler behind the same withLease, so a budget on either covers the batch.
workerBatchScope.watermarkNote: A RATCHET, not a target. It is the count of derived cron batches carrying no budget at the commit that recorded it. The gate fails when the count RISES, so a new scheduled sweep must declare its five ceilings or be named below with a reason. Lowering it is the work; raising it to go green is the defect the ratchet exists to catch.

declaredOutOfScope./cron/outbox-events-metrics: not a batch: OutboxPublisherService.metrics() -> OutboxReportService.metrics(), a read of publisher counters. It drains nothing, claims no rows and writes nothing.
declaredOutOfScope./cron/outbox-events-report: not a batch: OutboxPublisherService.report() -> OutboxReportService.report(), a read. NOTE it accumulates one object per tenant in memory (outbox-report.service.ts:71-95) and is HTTP-reachable, which is a size finding raised in ticket 23 box 7, not a budget one.

read-path-explain.what: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) of the route's dominant read, run as the non-BYPASSRLS app role with app.organization_id set.
read-path-explain.caveat: Buffer blocks are environment-independent and are the number that ratchets. The millisecond percentiles are taken on loopback Postgres, so they exclude pool wait and network round trip and are a LOWER BOUND on production latency — they are never written into measuredLatencyP95Ms, which is the end-to-end application ceiling and stays unmeasured until an HTTP-level harness fills it.

db-call-count.what: QueryTelemetryTracker statement count around a real service/route invocation (src/db/query-telemetry.ts).

http-harness.what: Real HTTP requests against a live Nest app on the seeded database as the non-owner app role with RLS live and Redis off, timed end to end. 40 samples per read, 12 per write, 5 post-forced-GC heap samples in a separate pass.
http-harness.caveat: measuredDbCalls is deliberately left to the db-call-count instrument: the capture's requestDbCalls is a strict superset of the handler statement count that maxDbCalls describes (authentication, permission resolution and module entitlement are in it), so it is recorded as requestDbCalls and never as measuredDbCalls. Latency is loopback, single-process, uncompressed and cache-cold, so it excludes pool wait, network and gzip — it is a lower bound on production latency and an upper bound on the cache-hit path.

GET /clients.note: Client account list. Cache-miss ceiling, counted statement-by-statement out of ClientAccountsService.getClientAccounts: the read itself is 2 — one relational findMany over client_accounts with the salesRep/assignedCrm column joins, and one count() over the same predicate, issued together in a Promise.all. The handler also runs tryBackfill, which registerAfterCommit defers past commit but still inside the request: backfillConvertedLeadsToClientAccounts is 1 execute, and backfillCrmAssignments is 2 selects plus ceil(unassigned / BULK_UPDATE_CHUNK 500) bulk updates, both skipped once nothing is unassigned. Steady state is therefore 5 (2 read + 1 backfill insert + 2 assignment probes) and the first request after a tenant gains unassigned accounts adds the chunked write. resolveClientsReadScope and membersWithPermission are access reads, not counted — the same convention GET /dashboard/personal set. The ceiling stays at 10 rather than being tightened to the counted 5, because the chunk term is unbounded in the number of unassigned accounts; tightening it would declare a ceiling the cold path can exceed on data alone. Read from the call path AND confirmed against a live statement count.
